prompt.1: What should the government do about child care and schools?
prompt.2: What should the province do about child care and public schools?
prompt.3: What should the province's priorities be for child care and for schools from kindergarten to Grade 12?
prompt.4: Which direction should the province take on child care and on schools from kindergarten to Grade 12?
prompt.5: Choose the priority for ChildCareBC, the province's child care program, and for kindergarten to Grade 12 (K-12) schools.

context.1: Child care costs families a lot. The province pays for some low-cost spots, but it has paused adding new ones to save money. Some parties want many more low-cost spots or free child care. Others want schools to focus on reading, math and testing.
context.2: Child care can cost families as much as rent. About one in ten licensed spaces costs $10 a day, and the province has paused new $10-a-day spaces for three years to save money. Some fast-growing school districts still rely on portable classrooms. Parties disagree on whether to expand child care, focus schools on basics, or hold spending.
context.3: About 10% of licensed child care spaces cost $10 a day. In 2026 the NDP government paused new $10-a-day spaces for three years. Some fast-growing school districts still use many portable classrooms. The Greens want free child care by 2031 and CentreBC wants 20,000 more $10-a-day spaces. In October the NDP promised more spaces and a fee cap, using federal money. The Conservatives and OneBC focus on testing, grades and the basics; the Conservatives add higher family benefits and some targeted spaces.
context.4: About 10% of licensed child care spaces cost $10 a day. In February 2026 the NDP government paused new $10-a-day enrolment for three years to fix the program's funding model. The Affordable Child Care Benefit still helps families with incomes up to $111,000. Fast-growing school districts still use portable classrooms.
context.5: New $10-a-day enrolment has been frozen since February 2026 (reported as a three-year freeze), and Budget 2026 adds $330 million over three years for child care. There were more than 16,000 such spaces in March 2025, against a target of 20,000. The Affordable Child Care Benefit continues for family incomes up to $111,000. Budget 2026 plans $3.9 billion over three years to build, renovate and seismically upgrade schools. On October 17 the NDP pledged $80 million for school-based before- and after-school spaces and $250 million toward a renegotiated Canada-BC child care deal. The Conservatives' October 18 platform costs its family and child care measures at $150 million a year. The Greens' October 13 platform costs child care at $260 million a year, not counting capital for new centres, and education at $587 million a year. CentreBC puts its education plan at about $2.0 billion plus $750 million in capital over four years, and funds child care from federal money, by the party's own figures.

text.1: This party made child care cheaper, then paused new low-cost spots. In October it promised more spots and a cap on fees. It has built schools, but some students still learn in portable classrooms.
text.3: The NDP created $10-a-day child care, then in 2026 froze new spaces for three years. On October 17 it promised 7,200 before- and after-school spaces ($80 million), $250 million to expand affordable child care with federal money, a wage grid for early childhood educators and a fee cap. It says it has built 250 schools, but some fast-growing districts still rely on portable classrooms. It made no new K-12 promise in 2026.
text.5: The NDP launched ChildCareBC in 2018 and had more than 16,000 $10-a-day spaces by March 2025, toward a goal of 20,000. In February 2026 it paused new enrolment and expansion, a freeze Global News reported as three years, and Budget 2026 adds $330 million over three years for child care. The party says it built 250 schools. Budget 2026 plans $3.9 billion over three years for school building and seismic upgrades. On October 17, 2026 it pledged $80 million for 7,200 before- and after-school spaces on school grounds, and $250 million in new provincial money to leverage federal funding in the Canada-BC child care renegotiation (deadline December 1) for a provincial wage grid for early childhood educators, more affordable spaces and 'a hard, universal fee cap like Ontario'. It gave no cap amount, space target or date. It made no new K-12 commitment in 2026.

text.1: This party wants letter grades, exams and shop class back. It would give families a bit more money for child care and some new spaces.
text.3: The Conservatives' platform would restore letter grades and provincial exams, bring back shop classes and repeal SOGI 123. On child care it promises higher family benefits, 24-hour spaces and $10-a-day spaces for the families most in need as the program grows, at $150 million a year, with no space target.
text.5: The Conservatives' October 18 platform would restore letter grades for Grades 4 to 9 and 'consistent, supervised, curriculum-based provincial examinations', focus on literacy and mathematics, bring back shop classes, further limit phones, give parents curriculum access and opt-out rights, repeal SOGI 123, expand school meals in high-need communities and offer a refundable activity credit of up to $500 per child. On child care it would cut rules that delay new spaces, make independent providers eligible for new $10-a-day spaces 'as the program expands', give those spaces first to families with the highest need, create 24-hour spaces for shift workers, raise the BC Family Benefit and the Affordable Child Care Benefit, and match the federal multigenerational home renovation credit, at $150 million a year at full cost. It sets no space target and no school capital plan beyond shop facilities in new schools.

text.1: This party wants free child care for all, better pay for child care workers, and food for every student.
text.3: The Greens would lift the freeze now, make child care free for all by 2031, pay early childhood educators $35 to $45 an hour and feed every student. Their platform costs child care at $260 million a year and education at $587 million a year.
text.5: On September 28, 2026, the Greens promised to lift the freeze 'immediately', make child care free for all by 2031 and pay early childhood educators $35 to $45 an hour by 2028. Their October 13 platform adds one point of registration for $10-a-day spaces, new spaces and priority registration for public, non-profit and Indigenous-led centres, closing the inclusive education funding gap, universal school food, a school supplies program, moving private school funding into public schools in phases and a moratorium on artificial intelligence in classrooms. Their Education Policy Brief adds a counsellor per 250 students. The platform costs child care at $260 million a year, not counting capital for new centres, and education at $587 million a year, and pays for its plans mainly with a tax on net wealth above $50 million.

text.1: This party wants many more low-cost child care spots, new classrooms, letter grades and more school counsellors.
text.3: CentreBC's October 10 platform adds 20,000 $10-a-day spaces by 2030 with federal money and 25,000 school seats by 2031, starting where portables are most common. It keeps class-size limits, funds a counsellor per 400 students and 1,500 more education assistants, and brings back letter grades. The party puts the cost at about $2 billion plus $750 million in capital.
text.5: The platform adds 20,000 $10-a-day spaces by 2030, with federal funds 'secured to 2031', and 25,000 school seats by 2031 using prefab additions and $750 million in capital. It keeps and funds class-size limits, moves to a counsellor per 400 students by 2030, adds 1,500 education assistants, brings in letter grades for Grades 4 to 9 from September 2028, publishes test results by school, caps tuition increases at 2% and sets a school artificial intelligence standard in 2027. Education costs about $2.0 billion over four years (party figure).

text.1: This party wants student testing, more say for parents, and no new child care spending.
text.3: OneBC would bring in standardized testing in reading, writing and math and a Parental Bill of Rights, and would remove SOGI 123, a teaching resource on sexual orientation and gender identity. It has no child care plan.
text.5: OneBC's priorities are standardized testing focused on reading, writing and mathematics, a Parental Bill of Rights, and removing SOGI 123 (a sexual orientation and gender identity resource) and 'politicized content' from classrooms. It has no child care, school building or post-secondary commitments, and its 25% tax cuts and four-year plan to balance the budget limit new spending.

scoring_rationale: Five options. a = OneBC (4): standardized testing, Parental Bill of Rights, no child care spending; Conservative 3 (shares the testing focus, and its platform gives parents curriculum access, notification and opt-out rights, but it adds modest child care measures and no Parental Bill of Rights). A teacher strike ban was removed from option a on October 13 because no party or news source for it was found; CentreBC 1 (published FSA results by school, nothing else). b = Conservative (4): basics-first with the letter grades, exams and shop classes in its October 18 platform and small, targeted child care measures inside a no-new-taxes frame (option b was rewritten on October 18 from 'no child care commitment'; other parties' scores on it were kept); OneBC 3; CentreBC 2 (the same letter grades Grades 4-9 and literacy and numeracy focus, but the opposite on child care); NDP 1 (it keeps the Affordable Child Care Benefit; nothing else matches). c = NDP record (4): it built $10-a-day and then froze it, and the freeze is still in force; its October 17 pledge adds 7,200 school-based spaces with $80 million of provincial money, but the wider expansion, wage grid and fee cap depend on a renegotiated federal deal, so c stays its closest option; Conservative 2 (keeps the Affordable Child Care Benefit and adds modest spaces as the program grows, but would not defend the program as is); CentreBC 1 (would lift the freeze, keeps building); OneBC 1. d = CentreBC's platform (4): 20,000 spaces, 25,000 seats, counsellors, letter grades; Green 3 (goes further on child care, shares counsellors and food, differs on grades and AI); NDP 3 (created $10-a-day, builds seats and on October 17 pledged more affordable spaces with federal money, but no 20,000 target, letter grades or counsellors; score changed Oct 18 after the NDP child care release); Conservative 2 (letter grades in Grades 4 to 9 and some new $10-a-day spaces overlap, but no 20,000 target, seat count or counsellors; score changed Oct 18 after the Conservative platform); OneBC 0. e = Green (4); CentreBC 2 (expands spaces and school food, not free care or an ECE wage grid); NDP 2 (an early childhood educator wage grid and a fee cap, not free care; score changed Oct 18 after the NDP child care release, matching CentreBC's 2 for expanding spaces). SOGI 123 is scored only in its own question. Symmetry: Conservative on a (3) and OneBC on b (3); Conservative on d (2) and CentreBC on b (2).
